message.reasoning:
I need to decide on an auction bid for SHORT_LINE.

Opponent p2 leads the SHORT_LINE auction at $84. I have $546 cash and am considering bidding up to $99, then mortgaging the property for $100 to gain cash.

If I fold, p2 wins at $84 and can mortgage Short Line for $100. That gives them a $16 arbitrage. If I bid up to $99 and mortgage immediately, I gain $1-$15 cash. The opponent has only $225 cash.

p2 already owns B&O Railroad, which is mortgaged. They do not own Reading or Pennsylvania. If they win Short Line, they would have only one active railroad plus a mortgaged B&O. That combination yields just $25 in rent, so bidding above the $100 mortgage value seems unwise.

I will bid $85 to match p2's current offer. I plan to raise by one dollar increments up to $99, then drop if the bid reaches $100 or above. This strategy drains their cash while keeping the mortgage arbitrage intact.

I am reconsidering the auction strategy. The opponent's dangerous properties include Park Place and Boardwalk with three houses each, plus an orange monopoly with four houses on each street. These yield lethal rent payments. My own light blue monopoly is weaker, so giving the opponent cash to buy Short Line may be unwise.

My light blue properties rent $450, $300, and $300. Cash is critical to survive the opponent's board.

Winning Short Line at $85 and mortgaging for $100 nets $15 cash. If the opponent bids to $100, mortgage value equals price and arbitrage disappears. I will bid $85 now and drop if they reach $100.

I am weighing whether to jump straight to $99 or continue the incremental war. Winning at $99 nets only a $1 arbitrage, while winning at $85 nets $15. Incremental bidding is preferable if the opponent drops early.

The opponent has been matching every bid, so they may be committed to bidding up to $99. The current sequence is odd-even: I bid 85, they bid 86, and so on. If I continue this pattern, I will reach $99 first while they would need to bid $100 to match. This means I can secure the property at $99 and still mortgage it for $100, gaining only a small arbitrage.

I will not jump straight to $99. The opponent has not dropped in 84 bids, so they are likely committed to continuing the incremental war. I will bid $85 and keep raising by one dollar until they reach $100.

Rational mortgage arbitrage suggests the opponent will not bid $100, since mortgaging immediately nets zero cash. I should secure Short Line at $99.

If I win, I would own three mortgaged railroads. Unmortgaging them costs 10% interest, which is too expensive given my cash needs.

Both players can afford to bid to $99. If I win at $89, I net $11 after mortgaging. If I let them win at $88, they gain $12 from the arbitrage. I must decide whether to push the bid higher or concede.
